questions.q: Fill in the blank: a network is a collection of interconnected devices that communicate and/or share ________.
questions.explain: A network is a collection of interconnected devices that communicate and/or share resources. Because of the 'and/or', devices may exchange messages, share something like a printer or file server, or do both.

questions.q: What makes a device an end device?
choices: It is the infrastructure that lets other devices communicate
It is the source or the destination of communication across a network
It is any device that a person interacts with directly
It sits at the edge of a WAN and connects it to LANs
questions.explain: End devices are the source or destination of communication. Users interact directly with many of them, but that is not the definition. A server is an end device even though nobody sits at it.

questions.q: Which of these are intermediary devices?
questions.explain: Modems, routers, switches and hubs are intermediary devices: data passes through them on its way somewhere else. File servers, IoT appliances such as smart refrigerators, and medical devices such as insulin pumps are end devices, because data starts or ends at them.

questions.q: A server is an intermediary device, because users do not interact with it directly.
questions.explain: A server is an end device. It is the destination of a client's request and the source of the reply. Whether a person uses the device directly does not decide the category.

questions.q: What role do intermediary devices play in a network?
choices: They are the infrastructure that lets end devices communicate, providing the connectivity that makes larger and/or long-distance networks possible
They are where communication starts and ends
They store the shared resources, such as files, that end devices request
They are the cables and wireless signals that carry the data
questions.explain: Intermediary devices (modems, routers, switches, hubs) are infrastructure. Communication starting and ending describes end devices, storing shared files describes a server (an end device), and cables or wireless signals are physical media, not devices.

questions.q: You load a web page on your laptop. The request goes through your home router and modem, across the Internet, to a web server. Which of these are end devices in this exchange?
questions.explain: The laptop is the source of the request and the web server is its destination (and the source of the reply). The router and modem only pass the data along, so they are intermediary devices.

questions.q: Only general-purpose computers such as desktops, laptops and servers can be part of a network.
questions.explain: Almost anything can be part of a network. Examples include smartphones and tablets, IoT devices (smart TVs, lights, refrigerators), wearables (smart watches, glasses) and personal medical devices (glucose monitors, insulin pumps, pacemakers).

questions.q: A smart TV, a smartwatch and a pacemaker are all examples of which kind of device?
questions.explain: These are end devices: an IoT device, a wearable and a personal medical device. Each one is the source or destination of the data it sends or receives.

questions.q: Which is the best description of a Local Area Network (LAN)?
choices: A group of devices in a local geographical location, such as a home or office building
A network of a few square feet at most that connects one person's devices
Multiple connected networks serving a university campus or military base
A network that spans multiple cities or states
questions.explain: A LAN is a group of devices in a local geographical location such as a home or office building. The other choices describe a PAN, a CAN and a WAN.

questions.q: A LAN has no strict size limit. Which two characteristics generally describe one?
choices: It is confined to a single room and uses only wireless media
It spans several cities and is shared by many organizations
It is confined to a small number of buildings and is owned and managed by a single entity
It must be wired with coaxial cable and serves only one person
questions.explain: A LAN is generally confined to a small number of buildings and is owned and managed by a single entity, such as one person, one company or one administration. The single owner is a big part of what separates it from larger networks.

questions.q: A LAN has a strict maximum size: once a network passes a certain number of devices or square feet, it is no longer a LAN.
questions.explain: There is no strict size limit to a LAN. It is characterized by covering a local area (generally a small number of buildings) and having a single owner or manager.

questions.q: A large medical complex has a separate LAN in each of its buildings, and those LANs are connected together. What kind of network is this?
questions.explain: A Campus Area Network (CAN) is multiple connected LANs serving a larger geographical location. Examples are a university campus, a military base, a large medical complex and a shopping mall.

questions.q: A city builds a network that connects its residents, school systems, public services and emergency responders. What kind of network is this?
questions.explain: A MAN is a much larger network that may serve an entire city or a section of a city. It connects residents, school systems, public services, emergency response and so on.

questions.q: A MAN serves an entire city or a section of a city. What does MAN stand for?
questions.explain: The module's slides expand MAN as Municipal Area Network. Many other sources call it a Metropolitan Area Network. Both names refer to the same city-scale network.

questions.q: Which pair of network types are formed by grouping multiple LANs together into a larger 'LAN of LANs'?
questions.explain: Campus Area Networks and Municipal Area Networks are both formed by grouping multiple LANs together. PANs, BANs and Nano networks are smaller than a LAN.

questions.q: How does a CAN differ from a MAN?
choices: A CAN connects LANs across one larger site, such as a campus, military base or mall. A MAN serves an entire city or a section of one.
A CAN uses only wireless media. A MAN uses only cables.
A CAN connects one person's devices. A MAN connects one building's devices.
A CAN spans multiple countries. A MAN is limited to one building.
questions.explain: Both are 'LANs of LANs', but at different scales. A CAN covers one larger site (university campus, military base, large medical complex, shopping mall). A MAN covers a city or part of a city.

questions.q: A public school connects its teacher and administrator workstations, printers, computer lab equipment and Chromebooks, all under one administration. What kind of network is this?
questions.explain: A public school is an example of a LAN: devices in a local area (a small number of buildings) owned and managed by a single entity.

questions.q: Which of these are examples of Campus Area Networks?
questions.explain: A university campus, a military base, a large medical complex and a shopping mall are all CAN examples. An individual's home is a LAN, and an entire city is a MAN.

questions.q: Which describes a Personal Area Network (PAN)?
choices: A very small network, generally a few square feet at most, that connects devices belonging to a single person
A home network whose devices connect through a modem and router
A network serving a section of a city
Any network that uses only wired media
questions.explain: A PAN is very small (a few square feet at most) and connects one person's devices: a laptop, a smartphone, wireless headsets, wearables and medical devices such as pacemakers.

questions.q: Which technologies are typically used to connect a PAN?
questions.explain: PANs generally use short-range technologies such as Bluetooth, Infrared (IR) and Near-Field Communication (NFC). Satellites and cable are the kind of permanent infrastructure that WANs rely on.

questions.q: You pair wireless earbuds with your phone and use Bluetooth to send a photo from the phone to your laptop. What type of network are these devices forming?
questions.explain: Connecting earbuds and mice, transferring files from a smartphone to a laptop, and synchronizing data are typical PAN uses. The devices belong to one person, sit within a few feet, and use a short-range technology (Bluetooth).

questions.q: Medical devices such as pacemakers can be part of a PAN. They may also be part of an even smaller network type. Give its acronym or full name.
questions.explain: A Body Area Network (BAN) covers devices on or in one person's body, such as a pacemaker. In the scale diagram it sits just inside the PAN.

questions.q: Which describes a Wide Area Network (WAN)?
choices: Multiple connected LANs on one university campus
A very large network that spans multiple cities, states, countries or continents
A city-wide network for residents and public services
Any network that contains more than one router
questions.explain: A WAN is a very large network spanning multiple cities, states, countries or continents. It connects many different LANs and other smaller networks.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a WAN?
choices: A home network with a modem and router
A phone paired with a smartwatch
questions.explain: The Internet is an example of a WAN. The others are a LAN, a PAN and a CAN.

questions.q: What kind of infrastructure do WANs rely on?
choices: Short-range technologies such as Bluetooth and NFC
More permanent and/or reliable infrastructure, such as copper or fiber optic cable and satellites
questions.explain: Because of the distances involved, WANs rely on more permanent and/or reliable infrastructure, such as cable (copper, fiber optic, etc.) and satellites. Short-range technologies are PAN territory.

questions.q: Which of these are typical uses of a WAN?
choices: A corporation linking offices in distant locations
An employee working remotely who connects to their organization's network from far away
Syncing a smartwatch with a phone
Sharing a printer within one office building
questions.explain: WANs serve large corporations with distant offices, remote employees, cloud services and anything else that needs connectivity over very large distances. Syncing a smartwatch is a PAN use, and sharing a printer in one office is a LAN use.

questions.q: Which list orders the network scopes from smallest to largest, as in the nested-circles scale diagram?
choices: Nano, BAN, PAN, LAN, CAN, MAN, RAN, WAN
Nano, PAN, BAN, LAN, CAN, MAN, RAN, WAN
Nano, BAN, PAN, LAN, MAN, CAN, RAN, WAN
BAN, Nano, PAN, LAN, CAN, RAN, MAN, WAN
questions.explain: From smallest to largest: Nano < BAN < PAN < LAN < CAN < MAN < RAN < WAN. Mnemonic: Nice Big Puppies Love Chewing My Red Wallet. Each larger scope can contain the smaller ones.

questions.q: In the nested-circles scale diagram, which scope sits directly between MAN and WAN?
questions.explain: The order is ... CAN < MAN < RAN < WAN. The slides show RAN only in the diagram and do not define it. Elsewhere it usually stands for Regional Area Network.

questions.q: Because WANs span such large distances, they typically link their LANs with short-range technologies like Bluetooth and NFC.
questions.explain: Short-range technologies like Bluetooth, IR and NFC are typical of PANs. WANs rely on more permanent and/or reliable infrastructure, such as copper or fiber optic cable and satellites.

questions.q: Regardless of a network's size, every device on it must be connected via some physical medium.
questions.explain: Every device on a network must be connected via some physical medium. That medium can be tangible (cables) or intangible (wireless).

questions.q: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth do not count as physical media, since nothing tangible connects the devices.
questions.explain: Physical media include intangible media: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Infrared, Zigbee and Cellular. They generally rely on radio waves or electromagnetic radiation.

questions.q: Which cable consists of copper wires twisted together and comes in categories such as Cat5e and Cat6?
questions.explain: Twisted pair cables (Cat5e, Cat6, etc.) are copper wires twisted together. This is the usual Ethernet cable.

questions.q: Which medium is a conducting cable surrounded by a metallic shield?
questions.explain: A coaxial cable is a conducting cable surrounded by a metallic shield.

questions.q: Which tangible medium carries signals as light rather than electricity?
questions.explain: Fiber optic cables are glass or plastic fibers that carry light signals. Twisted pair and coaxial carry electrical signals over a conductor.

questions.q: You are shown a round, thick black cable that ends in a screw-on metal connector with a single copper pin in the center. Which cable is it?
questions.explain: That is a coaxial cable. Twisted pair shows several colored pairs of thin wires twisted together inside a jacket, and fiber optic shows a bundle of many hair-thin strands.

questions.q: Which of these are intangible (wireless) media?
questions.explain: The intangible media are Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Infrared (IR), Zigbee and Cellular. Coaxial, Cat6 (twisted pair) and fiber optic are tangible, wired media.

questions.q: What do wireless media generally rely on to carry signals?
questions.explain: Wireless media generally rely on radio waves or electromagnetic radiation. A footnote adds that other options exist, such as quantum entanglement.

questions.q: Which tangible media carry electrical signals over a conductor?
questions.explain: Twisted pair (copper wires) and coaxial (a shielded conductor) carry electrical signals. Fiber optic carries light through glass or plastic fibers.

questions.q: What is network topology?
choices: The geographic area a network covers
The layout of the connections between devices on a network
The physical medium a network uses
The number of devices on a network
questions.explain: Network topology is the layout of the connections between devices on a network. The geographic area describes a network's scope (LAN, WAN, etc.), not its topology.

questions.q: Devices on a network (computers, servers, routers, etc.) are called nodes. Using graph-theory terms, what else are nodes called?
questions.explain: Nodes are also called vertices (singular: vertex). Connections are also called edges or links. These terms come from graph theory, since a network diagram is a graph.

questions.q: The media through which nodes communicate are called connections. What other names are used for them?
questions.explain: Connections are also called edges or links, depending on context. Vertices is another name for nodes, and hubs are intermediary devices.

questions.q: Which list names the qualities that decisions about network topology affect?
questions.explain: Topology decisions affect performance, reliability, fault-tolerance and scalability. Area, resources and purpose are how networks are classified by scope.

questions.q: What does fault-tolerance mean for a network?
choices: How quickly packets can be sent across it
Its capacity to keep functioning when components are compromised, for example when a connection is broken
How readily it can be expanded
The number of collisions it experiences
questions.explain: Fault-tolerance is the capacity for a network to keep functioning when components are compromised, such as a broken connection. Packet speed and collisions fall under performance, and expansion is scalability.

questions.q: What does a network's performance refer to?
choices: The capacity to keep working when a connection breaks
How cheaply and easily the network can be expanded
How large a geographic area the network covers
The speed and efficiency of the network: how quickly packets cross it, the amount of latency, collisions, etc.
questions.explain: Performance is the speed and efficiency of the network: how quickly packets can be sent across it, how much latency there is, how many collisions occur, and so on.

questions.q: Adding a new wing of devices to a network would require costly new equipment, complex reconfiguration and a day of downtime. Which aspect of scalability does this concern?
questions.explain: Scalability can consider overhead (the cost, complexity and downtime of expanding) and/or behavior (how performance, fault-tolerance, etc. hold up as the network grows). Cost, complexity and downtime are overhead.

questions.q: A network is cheap and easy to expand, but as it grows from 5 to 50 devices its latency and collisions rise sharply. In which sense does it scale poorly?
questions.explain: Expanding is easy, so overhead scalability is good. Performance degrading as the network grows is poor behavior scalability. The bus topology is the standard example of this.

questions.q: What is a collision on a network?
choices: Two devices send on the same shared medium at the same time, their signals interfere, and the data has to be resent
A device receives data that was meant for another device
A connection breaks and the network stops working
Two networks overlap in geographic scope
questions.explain: A collision happens when two devices transmit on the same shared medium at the same time and their signals interfere, so the data must be sent again. The more devices share one medium, the more collisions occur.

questions.q: Latency is best described as:
choices: The maximum number of devices a network supports
The ability of a network to keep working after a failure
Delay: how long data takes to get from source to destination
The cost of expanding a network
questions.explain: Latency is delay, the time data takes to get from source to destination. Each intermediate device the data passes through adds some.

questions.q: What is a point-to-point network?
choices: Many devices sharing a single cable
A bus whose ends are connected
A network that links exactly two devices via a direct connection between them
Two LANs joined by a router
questions.explain: Point-to-point is the most basic physical topology. It links exactly two devices with a direct connection between them.

questions.q: Why do point-to-point networks generally have high performance?
choices: Nothing else competes for bandwidth, and there are no intermediate devices to add latency
Data can travel in either direction, so it takes the shorter path
They always use fiber optic cable
questions.explain: Only the two devices use the link, so nothing competes for bandwidth. The connection is direct, so no intermediate devices add latency. The token and the two directions belong to ring topologies.

questions.q: Since point-to-point is the most basic topology, it generally has low performance.
questions.explain: Point-to-point is the most basic topology, but its performance is generally high: no competition for bandwidth and no intermediate devices. Its weaknesses are fault tolerance (none) and scalability (none).

questions.q: How fault tolerant is a point-to-point network?
choices: High, because either device can take over if the other fails
Moderate, because data can be rerouted the other way
Nonexistent: either the devices and the link work, or they don't
The same as a bidirectional ring
questions.explain: Fault tolerance is nonexistent. There is a single link and no backup path, so if either device or the link fails, the network fails.

questions.q: Why does a point-to-point topology not scale?
choices: Each new device lowers its performance noticeably
By definition it links exactly two devices, so adding a third makes it no longer point-to-point
Its cable has a strict length limit
New devices must wait for a token
questions.explain: Point-to-point topologies do not scale by definition. The topology is exactly two devices and one direct link.

questions.q: Which topology has high performance but no fault tolerance and no scalability?
questions.explain: Point-to-point: high performance (no competition, no intermediates), nonexistent fault tolerance, and no scaling by definition.

questions.q: How does a bus topology connect its devices?
choices: With a direct link between every pair of devices
With a closed loop that a token travels around
With a single, shared medium such as a cable
With exactly one direct connection between two devices
questions.explain: A bus topology connects many devices via a single, shared medium, such as a cable.

questions.q: Which of these are advantages of a bus topology?
choices: Performance holds steady as devices are added
questions.explain: Like point-to-point, a bus is extremely simple, quick to set up, needs minimal resources and is easily expanded. However, it has little fault tolerance, and performance decreases noticeably as more devices are added.

questions.q: A bus topology can be described as both 'easily expanded' and 'scaling poorly' without contradiction.
questions.explain: Scalability has two senses. A bus has low overhead to expand (just tap another device onto the cable), but its behavior worsens as it grows, because performance drops as more devices share the medium.

questions.q: Why does a bus network's performance drop noticeably as devices are added?
choices: The token takes longer to travel around the loop
All devices share one medium, so they compete for bandwidth and collide more often
The cable must be replaced each time a device is added
Each new device becomes an intermediary device
questions.explain: Every device on a bus shares the same medium. More devices means more competition for bandwidth and more collisions.

questions.q: The single shared cable in a bus network is cut. What is the likely result?
choices: Data automatically reroutes the other way around
Nothing changes, because each device has its own direct link to every other device
The network is disrupted, since every device depends on the one shared cable
Performance improves, because fewer devices compete for bandwidth
questions.explain: A bus has little fault tolerance. Everything depends on the one shared medium, so a break in it disrupts the network.

questions.q: A ring topology is essentially:
choices: A point-to-point link between exactly two devices
A bus topology with the ends connected
A set of LANs grouped into a LAN of LANs
A bus with a second, backup cable running alongside it
questions.explain: A ring topology is essentially a bus topology with the ends connected.

questions.q: In a ring topology, data can only travel in one direction around the ring.
questions.explain: Depending on its structure, a ring can pass data unidirectionally (one way) or bidirectionally (both ways).

questions.q: In a ring topology, what does the token act like?
choices: A 'talking stick': only the device holding it may transmit
An address label attached to every packet
A backup cable used when a link breaks
questions.explain: A token travels around the ring and acts as a sort of 'talking stick'. Only the device holding it transmits, so two devices never send at once.

questions.q: The token reaches a device that has no data to send. What happens next?
choices: The token waits at that device until it has data
The device transmits an empty packet
The token moves on to the next device
The token is destroyed and a new one is created
questions.explain: The token checks whether a device needs to transmit. If it does, the device transmits. If not, the token moves on to the next device.

questions.q: What problem does token passing help prevent?
questions.explain: Only the token holder can transmit, so two devices never send on the ring at the same time. This helps prevent collisions.

questions.q: Unidirectional rings have the same general downsides as which topology?
choices: None: they have no real downsides
questions.explain: Unidirectional rings have the same general downsides as a bus: little fault tolerance and performance limits. There is only one path, so one break stops the ring.

questions.q: Why do bidirectional rings have greater fault tolerance and lower latency than unidirectional rings?
choices: They use a token, which unidirectional rings lack
They always use fiber optic cable
They have multiple channels, so data can travel either way around the ring
questions.explain: Bidirectional rings have multiple channels. If one link breaks, data can go around the other way (fault tolerance), and data can take whichever direction is shorter (lower latency). The token is a feature of rings in general.

questions.q: In a bidirectional ring, the link between two neighboring devices breaks. What happens to traffic that would have used that link?
choices: It can still reach its destination by traveling the other way around the ring
The whole ring stops, just like a bus with a cut cable
It waits at the break until the link is repaired
It is carried by the token instead
questions.explain: A bidirectional ring has multiple channels, so a single break does not stop it. Data goes around the other way. That is why it has greater fault tolerance than a unidirectional ring.

questions.q: A unidirectional ring has 8 devices (and 8 links), and data flows only clockwise. A device sends data to its neighbor immediately counterclockwise from it. How many links must the data cross to arrive?
questions.explain: Data can only go clockwise, so it must travel almost all the way around: 7 of the 8 links. In a bidirectional ring it could go counterclockwise and cross just 1 link. This is why bidirectional rings have lower latency.
